metadata.title: Influence of students’ perceptions of instruction quality on their digital reading performance in 29 OECD countries: A multilevel analysis

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata with a three-level nested structure (students within schools within countries) and applies student weights normalized and specified in the HLM models to obtain unbiased estimates, following OECD guidance for PISA analyses. The analytic sample includes 29 OECD countries and 223,807 students from 8,692 schools, after excluding 94 schools (1,956 students) due to inconsistencies between school type from questionnaires and administrative records. The dependent variable is based on PISA’s digital reading plausible values, and the authors run analyses separately for each PV and pool results using Rubin’s rules. No replicate-weight scheme (e.g., BRR/jackknife) is reported, and the paper does not describe any additional weighting beyond the normalized student weights used in the multilevel modeling.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 computer-based reading assessment data for students in participating OECD countries, restricting to countries with available student, school, and country-level variables required for the models. Excluded 7 OECD countries because of missing school information (Austria, Belgium, Canada, New Zealand, Norway, Sweden) and missing educational expenditure data (Switzerland). Further excluded 94 schools (1,956 students) because of inconsistencies between school type derived from the school questionnaire and that from administrative records. For missingness, assumed missingness for LMINS was random due to rotated booklet design and random assignment, and applied multiple imputation with predictive mean matching to generate 10 complete datasets.

confounders_identified.variable_name: Principal perception of teacher digital skills

main_findings.target_variable: Digital reading performance (PVs pooled via Rubin’s rules)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Three-level HLM (random-intercept, fixed-slope) on PVs pooled with Rubin’s rules. Fixed-effect estimates (β, SE, p) reported in Table 4; random-effect variance explained via f2: student-level f2=8.859%, school-level f2=45.706%, country-level f2=14.117%. No ML classification/regression metrics (e.g., RMSE/AUC) reported.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Digital Reading the study leveraged adaptation of instruction, stimulation of reading engagement, teacher-directed instruction, training exercises for reading skills, and disciplinary climate in lessons to predict digital reading performance (PVs pooled via Rubin’s rules), finding that adaptation and engagement stimulation were positively associated with performance (β=0.067, p<0.001), while teacher-directed instruction and reading-skill training exercises were negatively associated (β=-0.084 and β=-0.094, p<0.001). This indicates that reading instruction quality should prioritize student-centered adaptation and engagement strategies while rethinking overreliance on drill-like reading exercises and teacher-directed approaches, though the relationships are correlational due to the cross-sectional PISA design.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 computer-based digital reading performance for 223,807 students (15-year-olds) across 29 OECD countries, using 10 plausible values for the outcome and pooling estimates with Rubin’s rules. It applies three-level hierarchical linear models (students within schools within countries) with normalized student weights and stepwise model building to retain statistically significant controls. Multiple imputation with predictive mean matching is used for missing LMINS (23.60%), generating 10 imputed datasets that are combined with PVs. In the final model, adaptation of instruction and stimulation of reading engagement show positive associations with digital reading (β=0.067, p<0.001), whereas teacher-directed instruction and training exercises for reading skills show negative associations (β=-0.084 and β=-0.094, p<0.001). Random effects indicate substantial school-level variance explained (f2=45.706%), and the authors caution that effect sizes are small and the design is correlational rather than causal.
